title: The Forgetting Curve
prompt: Ebbinghaus memorized lists of nonsense syllables, then tested himself later. How much did he still retain after each delay, up to a month?
source: Ebbinghaus, H. (1885). Über das Gedächtnis [Memory: A Contribution to Experimental Psychology].
takeaway: Almost half was gone within an hour — but after the first day, forgetting nearly flattens out.
note: Values from Ebbinghaus's savings table (20 min, 1 h, 9 h, 1, 2, 6 and 31 days).

title: The Keeling Curve
prompt: Atmospheric CO₂ has been measured continuously at Mauna Loa, Hawaii since 1958. Sketch the yearly average from 1959 to 2023.
source: Keeling, C. D. (1960). The concentration and isotopic abundances of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. Tellus, 12(2). Annual means: NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory.
takeaway: It isn't just rising — it's accelerating: about 0.8 ppm per year in the 1960s vs. about 2.4 ppm per year lately.
note: Annual means, rounded; the seasonal wiggle is smoothed out.

title: The Serial Position Effect
prompt: People hear a list of 20 words, then recall as many as they can in any order. How likely is each word to be recalled, by its position in the list?
source: Murdock, B. B. (1962). The serial position effect of free recall. Journal of Experimental Psychology, 64(5), 482–488.
takeaway: A U-shape: the first words get rehearsed (primacy) and the last ones are still in short-term memory (recency). The middle is a memory dead zone.
note: Approximate, digitized from the 20-word list condition.

title: The Age–Crime Curve
prompt: How does the arrest rate change across the lifespan? Show it as a percentage of the peak age's rate.
source: Hirschi, T., & Gottfredson, M. (1983). Age and the explanation of crime. American Journal of Sociology, 89(3), 552–584.
takeaway: A sharp spike in the late teens, then a long decline — a shape that shows up across eras and countries.
note: Approximate shape based on U.S. arrest data, rescaled to the peak.

title: Sleep Across the Lifespan
prompt: How many hours of sleep per day do people get, from newborns to age 85?
source: Roffwarg, H. P., Muzio, J. N., & Dement, W. C. (1966). Ontogenetic development of the human sleep-dream cycle. Science, 152(3722), 604–619.
takeaway: Most of the drop happens in childhood. Adulthood is a slow slide — and later research suggests older adults lose less than this classic figure shows.
note: Age-group values from the classic figure, plotted at group midpoints.

title: World Population
prompt: Sketch the number of people alive on Earth from 1800 to 2023.
source: United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs (2022). World Population Prospects 2022; historical estimates compiled by Our World in Data.
takeaway: It took all of human history to reach 1 billion (around 1800), and only 12 years to go from 7 to 8 billion.
note: Rounded estimates.

title: Global Temperature
prompt: How has global average surface temperature changed since 1880, compared with the 1951–1980 average? (Smoothed, so ignore year-to-year noise.)
source: Hansen, J., Ruedy, R., Sato, M., & Lo, K. (2010). Global surface temperature change. Reviews of Geophysics, 48(4). Data: NASA GISTEMP v4.
takeaway: Roughly flat with wobbles until the 1970s, then a steady climb — most of the warming has happened in the last 50 years.
note: Approximate smoothed values.

title: How Corn Grows
prompt: A Midwest farmer plants field corn. How tall is the plant over the first three months after planting?
source: Abendroth, L. J., Elmore, R. W., Boyer, M. J., & Marlay, S. K. (2011). Corn Growth and Development (PMR 1009). Iowa State University Extension.
takeaway: An S-curve: almost nothing for weeks, a stalk-elongation sprint of 2–3 inches a day, then height stops at about 8½ feet once the tassel emerges.
note: Approximate typical growth curve; actual timing depends on hybrid and temperature.

title: Conformity and Group Size
prompt: In Asch's line-judging experiments, a group of actors unanimously gave an obviously wrong answer. How often did the real participant go along with them, depending on how many actors there were?
xLabel: Number of people in the wrong majority
source: Asch, S. E. (1956). Studies of independence and conformity: I. A minority of one against a unanimous majority. Psychological Monographs, 70(9).
takeaway: Conformity jumps at three people, then plateaus — a crowd of 15 is no more persuasive than a group of 3.
note: Approximate values as commonly reported from Asch's group-size variation.

title: 8th-Grade Math Scores
prompt: Every 8th-grader in a national U.S. sample takes the same math test (scored 0–500). Draw the shape of the score distribution.
source: National Center for Education Statistics (2022). NAEP Mathematics, Grade 8 (The Nation's Report Card).
takeaway: Close to a bell curve, centered near 275 with a slightly longer tail toward low scores — the gap between the 10th and 90th percentile is about 100 points.
note: Approximate shape fitted to the published 2022 percentiles (10th ≈ 222, 50th ≈ 276, 90th ≈ 323).

title: How Tall Are Adults?
prompt: Take every adult in the U.S. — men and women together. Draw the shape of the height distribution.
source: Schilling, M. F., Watkins, A. E., & Watkins, W. (2002). Is human height bimodal? The American Statistician, 56(3), 223–229. Means/SDs: CDC NHANES 2015–2018.
takeaway: Not two humps! Men (about 5′9″) and women (about 5′3½″) differ by about 5½ inches, but that's too small relative to the spread within each group to split the curve.
note: 50/50 mixture of two normal curves using NHANES means and SDs, converted to inches.

title: Old Faithful's Eruptions
prompt: Yellowstone's Old Faithful geyser erupts many times a day. Draw the distribution of how long each eruption lasts.
source: Azzalini, A., & Bowman, A. W. (1990). A look at some data on the Old Faithful geyser. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C, 39(3), 357–365.
takeaway: Two clear humps — short (about 2 min) and long (about 4.5 min) eruptions — and almost nothing in between.
note: Two-component normal fit to the classic 272-eruption data set.

title: Reaction Times
prompt: People press a button as fast as possible when a light flashes, over and over. Draw the distribution of their reaction times.
source: Luce, R. D. (1986). Response Times: Their Role in Inferring Elementary Mental Organization. Oxford University Press.
takeaway: Strongly right-skewed: there's a hard floor on how fast you can be, but lapses of attention produce a long tail of slow responses.
note: Approximate, using a typical ex-Gaussian shape for simple visual reaction time.

title: Household Income
prompt: Draw the distribution of yearly U.S. household income (0 to $250k).
source: Guzman, G., & Kollar, M. (2023). Income in the United States: 2022 (Report P60-279). U.S. Census Bureau.
takeaway: The most common incomes sit well below the median ($74.6k), and a long right tail drags the mean up to about $106k.
note: Approximate log-normal fit matching the published median and mean.

title: Benford's Law
prompt: Take thousands of numbers from real life — river lengths, populations, street addresses. What share start with each first digit, 1 through 9?
source: Benford, F. (1938). The law of anomalous numbers. Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society, 78(4), 551–572.
takeaway: Not 11% each! About 30% start with 1 and under 5% with 9 — forensic accountants use this to spot made-up numbers.
note: Values from Benford's law, log₁₀(1 + 1/d), which matched Benford's 20,229 observations.

title: Milgram's Obedience Study
prompt: 40 men were told to give a 'learner' increasingly strong electric shocks (the shocks were fake). How many stopped at each level, out of 40?
source: Milgram, S. (1963). Behavioral study of obedience. Journal of Abnormal and Social Psychology, 67(4), 371–378.
takeaway: Nobody stopped before 300 volts, and 26 of 40 (65%) went all the way to the maximum — far more than psychiatrists predicted.
note: Counts from Table 2 of the original paper.

title: Zipf's Law of Words
prompt: In a million words of published American English, what share of all words is each of the 10 most common words?
source: Kučera, H., & Francis, W. N. (1967). Computational Analysis of Present-Day American English (Brown Corpus). Zipf, G. K. (1949). Human Behavior and the Principle of Least Effort.
takeaway: 'The' alone is 7% of everything we write — about twice as common as 'of', the #2 word, just as Zipf's law predicts.
note: Rounded frequencies from the Brown Corpus.

title: The Bystander Effect
prompt: Over an intercom, participants hear another participant having a seizure. What % went for help before the seizure ended, depending on how many people they thought were listening?
xLabel: People who could hear (including the participant)
source: Darley, J. M., & Latané, B. (1968). Bystander intervention in emergencies: Diffusion of responsibility. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 8(4), 377–383.
takeaway: More bystanders, less help: responsibility gets diffused, and each person assumes someone else has it handled.
note: Group-size labels count the participant, the victim and the other imagined listeners.

title: Leading Questions
prompt: People watch a film of a car crash, then are asked 'About how fast were the cars going when they ___ each other?' What was the average speed estimate for each verb?
source: Loftus, E. F., & Palmer, J. C. (1974). Reconstruction of automobile destruction. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 13(5), 585–589.
takeaway: One word changed the estimate by almost 9 mph. A week later, the 'smashed' group was also more than twice as likely to falsely remember broken glass.
note: Means from Table 1 of the original paper.

title: The Preston Curve
prompt: Each country is a dot: income per person vs. life expectancy. Draw the trend line through the cloud of countries.
xLabel: GDP per person ($ thousands, adjusted for prices)
source: Preston, S. H. (1975). The changing relation between mortality and level of economic development. Population Studies, 29(2), 231–248. Modern values: World Bank (2019).
takeaway: Steep then flat: the first $10k per person buys about 13 extra years of life; going from $40k to $80k buys about 2.
note: Approximate trend through 2019 country data.

title: Regression to the Mean
prompt: Galton measured hundreds of families. Draw the trend: the parents' average height vs. their adult children's height.
source: Galton, F. (1886). Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature. Journal of the Anthropological Institute, 15, 246–263.
takeaway: The slope is only about 2/3: very tall parents have tall kids, but not quite as tall. Galton named the effect 'regression' — the origin of the word.
note: Trend line with slope ≈ 0.65 through the mean (≈ 5′8″); female heights were scaled by 1.08 as Galton did.

title: Hubble's Expanding Universe
prompt: Hubble measured how far away galaxies are and how fast they move toward us (negative) or away from us (positive). Draw the trend line.
source: Hubble, E. (1929). A relation between distance and radial velocity among extra-galactic nebulae. PNAS, 15(3), 168–173.
takeaway: The farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes — evidence that the universe is expanding. (Hubble's slope was about 7× too steep because his distances were off; today's value is about 13 miles per second per million light-years.)
note: Hubble's fitted line (500 km/s per megaparsec), converted to about 95 miles per second per million light-years.

title: The Dunning–Kruger Effect
prompt: Students took a logical reasoning test, then guessed how they did compared to their peers. Split by actual quartile: how did they really score and how did they think they scored (as percentiles)?
source: Kruger, J., & Dunning, D. (1999). Unskilled and unaware of it. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 77(6), 1121–1134.
takeaway: Everyone thought they were above average. The bottom group overestimated by about 50 points, while the top group slightly underestimated themselves.
note: Approximate, digitized from the logical reasoning study (Study 2) figure.

title: Memory Underwater
prompt: Scuba divers learned 36 words either on the beach or 20 feet underwater, then were tested on land or underwater. How many words did each group recall?
source: Godden, D. R., & Baddeley, A. D. (1975). Context-dependent memory in two natural environments: On land and underwater. British Journal of Psychology, 66(3), 325–331.
takeaway: A crossover interaction: you remember best in the place you learned — about 40% more words when the settings matched.
note: Mean words recalled from the original paper.
